lead: Additive manufacturing (AM) builds a solid part from a 3D model by adding material layer by layer. It exists because it removes part-specific moulds, dies and fixtures, so one machine can make different shapes by changing the CAD file. It is used for prototypes, jigs, custom implants and small batches of end-use parts. Some syllabi call the whole group 3D printing; that is an umbrella term, not one process. The standard classification below is by how each layer is formed.
prereq: You need: Unit 3 basics of plastics and a general manufacturing overview; the process chain is in Chapter 7.2.

blocks.text: Additive manufacturing (AM) makes a part by adding material in thin layers. A 3D model is sliced into cross-sections. The machine builds each cross-section and bonds it to the previous one. Machining removes material; casting and forming need a mould or die. AM needs no part-specific tooling, so a new shape needs only a new CAD file.

In the 1980s, layer-by-layer machines made polymer models for shape checking. That use was called rapid prototyping (RP). Better lasers, powders and controls later allowed functional polymer, metal and ceramic parts. The broader term AM covers models, tools and end-use parts. Some syllabi call the whole group 3D printing. The CAD-to-part chain is in Chapter 7.2.
AM is classified by how each layer is formed, not only by material. This matters because the same material can be printed by more than one family. The next section lists the seven standard families.

The seven families differ in the state of the material and the energy source. Vat photopolymerisation cures a liquid resin with light. Material extrusion pushes a melted thermoplastic filament through a nozzle. Powder bed fusion fuses selected powder with a laser or electron beam. Material jetting deposits liquid droplets from printheads. Binder jetting deposits a binder into a powder bed. Sheet lamination bonds and cuts thin sheets. Directed energy deposition feeds powder or wire into a laser melt pool. A material such as nylon can appear in more than one family.

Common examples: stereolithography (SLA), fused deposition modelling (FDM), selective laser sintering (SLS), selective laser melting (SLM), multi-jet modelling (MJM), laminated object manufacturing (LOM) and laser engineered net shaping (LENS).

blocks.text: AM pays off when tooling would dominate the cost. A mould, die or fixture is needed for every design change in conventional routes. AM uses the same machine for many shapes. This gives four benefits.

items: No part-specific tooling: one-offs and small batches avoid mould cost.
Complex internal channels: curved cooling channels and lattice shapes can be built inside a part.
Low-volume production: spare parts can be made on demand instead of stored.
Mass customisation: each part can have its own CAD file, as in dental aligners.

blocks.text: The limits are equally real. Build speed is low, and the machine envelope limits part size. Surface finish is often rough, and support or powder removal adds labour. Material cost is high and the choice is narrower than conventional grades. Anisotropy means properties differ along the build direction because layers bond; a test bar in one direction may not represent another. For a small batch, compare total cost, not only machine price. Rapid tooling and end-use AM are in Chapter 7.9.

examples.question: A bracket needs a small batch. CNC setup costs ₹15,000 and each part costs ₹2,000; AM setup costs ₹2,000 and each part costs ₹3,500. Find the break-even batch size and which route is cheaper for 5 parts.
steps: Let n be the batch size in parts. CNC cost is C<sub>C</sub> = 15,000 + 2,000n rupees. AM cost is C<sub>A</sub> = 2,000 + 3,500n rupees.
n = 13,000 ÷ 1,500 = 8.666..., which rounds to 8.67 parts. Since parts are whole, AM is cheaper up to 8 parts and CNC is cheaper from 9 parts.
examples.answer: The break-even batch size is about 8.67 parts; for 5 parts AM costs ₹19,500 against CNC ₹25,000, so AM is cheaper by ₹5,500.
examples.check:
setup_cnc = 15000
part_cnc = 2000
setup_am = 2000
part_am = 3500
n = 5
breakeven = (setup_cnc - setup_am) / (part_am - part_cnc)
am_cost = setup_am + part_am * n
cnc_cost = setup_cnc + part_cnc * n
print(round(breakeven, 2))
print(int(am_cost))
print(int(cnc_cost))
print(int(cnc_cost - am_cost))

traps: Do not classify AM only by material. The standard families are by layer-forming mechanism; nylon, for example, can be used in powder bed fusion and material extrusion.
3D printing is an umbrella term, not one process. Do not use it as a synonym for FDM alone.
Rapid prototyping is not the same as all AM. RP is the early model-making use; AM also covers tools and end-use parts.
AM is not automatically cheaper. Setup is low but per-part cost is high; check the break-even batch size, and include support removal and post-processing.
Do not ignore anisotropy. Properties differ along the build direction, so one test direction does not certify the part.

quiz.q: Define additive manufacturing. Why is the process called additive?
quiz.a: AM builds a solid part from a 3D model by adding material layer by layer. It is called additive because material is joined or added, not removed as in machining.

quiz.q: Name the seven standard AM process families.
quiz.a: Vat photopolymerisation, material extrusion, powder bed fusion, material jetting, binder jetting, sheet lamination, directed energy deposition.

quiz.q: Why is AM classified by layer-forming mechanism rather than only by material? Give one material example.
quiz.a: The mechanism controls how layers bond, the support needed, accuracy and properties. The same material can be processed by different families; nylon can be used in powder bed fusion or material extrusion.

quiz.q: A bracket runs on CNC or AM. CNC setup ₹10,000 and each part ₹1,500; AM setup ₹3,000 and each part ₹3,000. Find the break-even batch size and the cheaper route for 3 parts.
A hydraulic manifold needs curved internal cooling channels. Explain why AM can make it and give one post-processing problem.
quiz.a: AM builds the channels as part of the sliced layers, so no mould core is needed. Powder or support trapped inside the channels must be removed, and internal surfaces may be rough.

quiz.q: State three benefits and three limits of AM.
quiz.a: Benefits: no part-specific tooling; complex internal channels; low-volume production or mass customisation. Limits: slow build and size limit; rough surface and support removal; high material cost; anisotropy.

quiz.q: Why does anisotropy matter when an AM part is compared with a machined wrought part?
quiz.a: AM properties depend on layer direction; strength and ductility along the build direction can differ from across layers. A machined wrought part is usually more uniform. Tests and design allowables must use the relevant direction.

quiz.q: Using the worked example costs (CNC: ₹15,000 setup + ₹2,000 per part; AM: ₹2,000 setup + ₹3,500 per part), compare 8 parts and 9 parts.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses AM for lightweight aerospace brackets, custom implants, and spare parts that are stored as CAD files. Research is moving toward multi-material printing, in-process monitoring, and qualification of metal parts for safety-critical use.
